evidence:
Probe at /tmp/gr149/u42/probe.py implements the three comparators and the two test shapes and prints the matrix:
  correct   (n>3)  row1(4/3)=True   row1(1/10)=True
  inverted  (n<=3) row1(4/3)=False  row1(1/10)=False
  inclusive (n>=3) row1(4/3)=False  row1(1/10)=True
Row 1 written with one and ten asserts (1 does not fire, 10 fires). Under the inverted comparator 1 fires and 10 does not, so BOTH assertions flip and the row fails. The inverting draft would not have passed it.
note: The sentence attributes to the inversion mutant what belongs to the boundary mutant. One and ten cannot separate n>3 from n>=3 — which is exactly what row 2's own mutant column (u36) says, correctly — but it separates n>3 from n<=3 as decisively as any pair can, because inverting a comparator inverts every verdict. So 'only asserting both sides of the boundary separates the two directions' is false twice over: the directions are separated by any pair straddling the threshold, and what both sides of the boundary separate is inclusive from exclusive, not one direction from the other. Row 2 is still worth writing; the paragraph justifying it argues from the wrong mutant, and it is the last paragraph of the spec — the one a reader carries away. Second, smaller: 'the threshold is the only number in this release' is not literally true (the release also turns on 'eight unit kinds' in §4), though it is true of the release's own arithmetic.
